articles.title: Locked out, shut in, left hungry: Afghanistan after Taliban takeover
articles.summary: Five years of Taliban rule have left Afghanistan with so much loss and so little hope. Women have been pushed out of sight and eventually mind.
articles.body: Five years of Taliban rule have left Afghanistan with so much loss and so little hope.Women have been pushed out of sight and eventually mind. Millions more face the threat of hunger as winter sets in.For a country that has already endured so much, hope is beginning to diminish.Since returning to power in August 2021, the Taliban has tightened its grip on everyday life, with women and girls bearing the brunt of its restrictions. Education, employment and freedom of movement have become increasingly difficult to access, while food insecurity, economic hardship, displacement and declining humanitarian assistance have deepened the crisis.“Today, the plight of many in Afghanistan is going from bad to worse,” UN Human Rights chief Volker Türk said, warning that the country's worsening situation was receiving inadequate international attention.“Yet, it seems the world has forgotten and abandoned the people of Afghanistan to a plight deepening by the day. The silence is deafening.”So, five years after the Taliban takeover, how has life changed for Afghans? Here are the numbers that tell the story.Living with over 100 decrees: How Afghan women are walking on eggshellsFor women living under the Taliban’s rule, everyday chores such as going to work, visiting a market, studying or seeking medical care have become a Herculean task.According to UN Women, more than 100 decrees targeting women and girls have been issued since the Taliban returned to power.It began with education. Girls were barred from secondary education beyond Grade 6, followed by the exclusion of women from universities.Then by July 2023, beauty salons, among the remaining sources of income and female-only social spaces, were ordered to shut. Women were also barred from parks, gyms and public bathhouses.Almost a year later, Taliban formalised its Law on the Propagation of Virtue and Prevention of Vice, imposing further controls on women's appearance and behaviour.Women were required to cover their bodies and faces in public and prohibited from raising their voices in public, including to sing or recite. Restrictions on employment, travel and dress, along with requirements to travel with a male guardian, further curtailed their freedom.And it's not just public life that the Taliban controls.In January 2026, the Taliban adopted a new Criminal Procedure Code for Courts that further highlighted the restrictions women face. Under Article 32, a husband who abuses his wife can face just 15 days in prison, and only if the abuse results in a broken bone, an open wound or a visible bruise.The code also allows husbands to impose discretionary punishments for “disobedience”, ranging from scolding to corporal punishment.Contrastingly, those who organise animal fights can face up to five months in prison.The restrictions have effectively shrunk women's everyday lives.According to a UN assessment, more than half of the women surveyed left home only once or twice a month. Nearly three-quarters felt unsafe leaving without a male guardian, while more than half avoided public spaces, including markets and healthcare facilities.Class dismissed: Afghanistan’s girls locked out of learningAfghanistan remains the only country in the world where girls and women are prohibited from accessing secondary and higher education under the current restrictions.According to UNICEF, more than 2.6 million girls had been denied secondary education since the Taliban takeover. Women had already been excluded from universities since December 2022, putting an end to an educational journey for millions.The consequences extend far beyond classrooms.Girls prevented from completing their education lose opportunities to pursue higher qualifications and skilled employment. Afghanistan, meanwhile, risks losing future teachers, doctors, nurses and other professionals needed to rebuild its institutions.The wider education system is also struggling. In January 2026, UNESCO and UNICEF reported that 93% of children completing primary school were still working towards basic reading proficiency.Between 2018 and 2024, the gross enrolment rate for boys fell from 120 to 104, while the rate for girls rose from 82 to 87. The overall rate declined from 101 to 95. Gross enrolment rates can exceed 100 because they include pupils outside the official age group and do not directly measure attendance or completion. The increase in girls' primary enrolment therefore does not mean restrictions on older girls have eased.The number of female teachers has also fallen, from 98,196 in 2019 to 66,208 in 2024, a decline of approximately 32.5%. UNICEF warned in April 2026 that Afghanistan could lose more than 25,000 female teachers and healthcare workers by 2030 if restrictions on girls' education and women's employment persist.The result could be a cycle of lost opportunity: girls are denied education today, fewer women qualify for professional jobs tomorrow, and future generations face a shrinking pool of trained educators and healthcare workers.No freedom and a huge mental tollThe loss of education, employment and freedom of movement has taken a psychological toll on Afghan women.UN Women reported in August 2026 that 70% of women surveyed described their mental health as bad or very bad. An earlier UNDP assessment, based on consultations conducted in 2024, found that 81% of women consulted rated their mental health as bad or very bad. The figures come from different assessments and should not be interpreted as a direct trend.The UNDP review identified excessive worry, hopelessness or hypervigilance among the most frequently reported behavioural changes, affecting 37% of respondents. Excessive sadness was reported by 22%, decreased appetite or sleep by 21%, fatigue by 20% and social withdrawal by 12%.These pressures are closely linked to restrictions on women's everyday lives. A student unable to return to school may see her future narrowing before she can choose a career. A woman who loses her job may lose both income and independence, while someone who rarely leaves home may have fewer opportunities to maintain friendships or seek support.Accessing mental-health services can itself be difficult because of movement restrictions, limited services and financial pressures on community organisations.UNICEF's 2025 humanitarian reporting said it provided mental-health and psychosocial support to more than 2.2 million children and caregivers through community-based and media initiatives.Women out of work: A deepening crisisInflation and job losses deepen economic hardshipAfghanistan's economic hardship has intensified as rising prices, job losses and cuts to international aid put further pressure on households.Inflation rose from an average of 3.6% in 2025 to 7.6% by March 2026, driven by higher food prices, supply disruptions and rising demand. Unemployment has almost doubled since 2021, according to the UN, while more than 500,000 jobs have disappeared.Women's exclusion comes at a steep economic costWomen face additional barriers to earning a living. UN Women estimated that only 7% of Afghan women were employed, compared with 84% of men. Their continued exclusion could cost the country $920 million cumulatively between 2024 and 2026, equivalent to 5.8% of GDP.Financial insecurity is particularly severe in female-headed households. UNDP's 2025 socio-economic review found that unstable sources accounted for 65% of income in these households in 2024, compared with 43% in male-headed households.Some women have turned to small businesses, but restrictions on mobility, access to markets and finance make running them difficult. Lost jobs, rising prices and limits on women's earnings leave families with fewer ways to absorb economic shocks.The damage could persist for years. UNICEF estimated in April 2026 that restrictions on girls' education and women's employment were costing Afghanistan at least $84 million annually in lost economic output. This estimate and UN Women's cumulative projection cover different periods and use different methodologies, so they should not be combined.Healthcare system left on ventilatorRestrictions on women's movement and a shortage of female medical professionals have made accessing treatment increasingly difficult.A February 2026 report by UN Special Rapporteur Richard Bennett found that movement restrictions, gender segregation and requirements to travel with a male guardian had severely limited women's access to healthcare. The absence of a male guardian could delay treatment even in emergencies.The shortage of female healthcare workers compounds the problem. Women were barred from medical and health education in December 2024, narrowing the pipeline of future doctors, nurses and midwives. In some regions, restrictions on women consulting male doctors make access to female medical professionals particularly important.Funding shortages have forced more than 440 health clinics to close or reduce services. The proportion of Afghans without access to healthcare rose from 16% in 2024 to 23% in 2025.Timely treatment is essential to prevent deaths from complications such as severe bleeding, high blood pressure, infections and obstructed labour. When women struggle to reach clinics or facilities that lack trained staff, the risks increase.Hunger games: Millions of Afghans have empty plateYears of economic hardship, drought and declining international aid have left millions of Afghans struggling to afford basic necessities.An October 2026 assessment by the Food and Agriculture Organization and the World Food Programme projected that 19.2 million people, or 38% of Afghanistan's population, would face acute food insecurity during November 2026-April 2027. This is up 10.3% from 17.4 million projected for the corresponding period a year earlier. Around five million people are expected to face emergency levels of hunger.Meanwhile, 21.9 million people, or about 45% of the population, are expected to need humanitarian assistance in 2026, including around 11.6 million children.Despite a relatively strong agricultural season, high food and transport costs, limited jobs, weak purchasing power, population movements and declining aid continue to undermine food access. Families may be forced to cut meals, buy less nutritious food or sacrifice other necessities, putting children and pregnant or breastfeeding women at particular risk.Child malnutrition deepens the crisisUNICEF reported in August 2026 that 3.7 million children were suffering from wasting, including around one million with severe acute malnutrition. Separately, supplied figures estimate that 3.5 million children under five are already experiencing acute malnutrition. These figures use different descriptions and require source checks before publication.Food-security assessments also projected that around four million women and children would need treatment for acute malnutrition in 2027, including approximately one million severe cases. These figures represent different measures and should not be added together.Funding shortages are already restricting access to help. The World Food Programme said in 2026 that it was turning away three out of four acutely malnourished children seeking assistance because it lacked funds to buy food.When the lifeline runs dry: Aid cuts leave Afghans in the lurcThe United States, previously Afghanistan's largest donor, provided more than $3 billion in humanitarian and development assistance between October 2021 and December 2024. In January 2025, US President Donald Trump suspended US humanitarian funding for Afghanistan, removing a source that had accounted for about 45% of humanitarian support.The 2026 Humanitarian Needs and Response Plan requires $1.71 billion to provide life-saving assistance and aims to reach 17.5 million people.As of August 2026, the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs had recorded US$509.3 million, or 29.7% of the appeal, leaving a shortfall of approximately US$1.20 billion.Funding gaps have forced aid organisations to reduce coverage, interrupt supplies and close service points. Women and girls are particularly vulnerable when specialist services become unavailable.UN Women reported in August 2026 that nearly three-quarters of women-led organisations surveyed had experienced funding cuts in 2025, while more than half expected to suspend operations or close within the following year.The consequences extend across food assistance, nutrition and healthcare. With millions needing support, agencies face increasingly difficult choices about distributing scarce resources.Five years, countless restrictions: Afghanistan’s shrinking worldFive years after the Taliban returned to power, Afghanistan is a country where everyday life has become a struggle for survival, dignity and hope. For women and girls, restrictions have turned once ordinary freedoms into distant possibilities.For millions of families, putting food on the table and accessing basic healthcare have become increasingly difficult. As economic hardship deepens and humanitarian support dwindles, the crisis is reaching into every corner of Afghan life.But what has changed since the Taliban takeover, and what does it mean for the country's future?The numbers paint a grim picture.You use AI every day. articles.title: In the mid-1990s, a New Mexico business owner bought 50 eroded acres; she planted more than 5,000 trees and shrubs to help restore its wetlands
articles.summary: Discover how Kimberly de Castro revitalized a barren 50-acre ranch in New Mexico by planting over 5,000 trees and shrubs, creating wetlands, and inspiring community conservation efforts.
articles.body: In the mid-1990s, Kimberly de Castro bought a 50-acre ranch outside San Jose, New Mexico. At the time, the land she purchased was overgrazed, eroded, and largely barren. Rather than abandoning the property, she began rehabilitating the land with help from a small grant through the US Fish and Wildlife Service’s Partners for Fish and Wildlife Program. The US Department of Interior’s 2002 annual report noted that de Castro planted more than 5,000 trees and shrubs, sowed grass seed, and placed straw bales containing seed and fertiliser in areas where erosion was most severe.Additionally, she developed and installed a five-mile drip-irrigation system to supply water to the new plants. Eventually, the project helped the ranch regain vegetation by dividing the property into distinct ecological zones: fragile riparian areas were fenced off to restore its wetlands, while the upland pastures were reclaimed to support separate, sustainable rotational grazing. This work also encouraged neighbouring landowners to undertake conservation works of their own. Decades later, looking back from 2026, this multi-layered rehabilitation serves as a historical case study in long-term private land management.How degraded land became a restoration projectWhen de Castro bought the ranch, the land’s condition showed the effects of intensive grazing and erosion. This was because the land was said to be windswept, overgrazed, and bare according to the government report. This kind of soil is not only difficult for plants to grow in, but the absence of vegetation on this soil means that it becomes susceptible to erosion. The response to this by de Castro was a combination of planting and soil-stabilisation measures instead of relying on a single intervention. Grass seed was drilled into the ground; straw bales containing seed and fertiliser were placed in badly eroded areas.The US Fish and Wildlife Service’s Partners for Fish and Wildlife Program, which works with private landowners to improve wildlife habitat on their property, provided a small grant for this project. The grant was one part of the restoration effort, alongside planting grass seedlings, erosion-control measures and irrigation.Planting thousands of trees and shrubsPlanting more than 5,000 trees and shrubs was a crucial part of de Castro’s work. However, the restoration involved more than just introducing new plants. The federal agency reported that the ranch eventually bloomed again, successfully supporting sustainable grazing on its reclaimed uplands while entirely preserving the adjacent wetlands. As the report does not provide a survival rate for the plantings or quantify changes in erosion, soil conditions or wildlife populations, it can best be described as the recovery of vegetation and the return of the property to productive grazing, instead of a measured ecological transformation.As noted in the historical records of the Department of the Interior, the project provided an impetus for the wider watershed community. The business owner's efforts encouraged dozens of neighbouring landowners to form a regional conservation collective, ultimately pooling their contiguous properties to extend similar resource-management work across a combined 5,000 acres of the shared valley. The extra lands were part of the wider community project. Moreover, de Castro involved teachers and pupils from the surrounding schools in the partnership.Wetland, wildlife and environmental educationAn account published by the US Environmental Protection Agency provides further context about the property’s conservation role. It reported that the 50-acre property included two restored wetlands and more than 5,000 plants. The wetland restoration formed part of the broader rehabilitation of the property, alongside planting and other land-management works.The wetland area can create habitats to sustain wildlife such as birds, fish and amphibians, as well as store and purify water. According to the guidelines provided by the EPA on the management of wetland and riparian areas, some of the roles played include habitat creation. Therefore, de Castro’s project began with the rehabilitation of a degraded 50-acre ranch and developed into a wider conservation effort involving neighbouring landowners and local schools.You use AI every day. articles.title: Work begins on new hotel and bar on site of landmark former Blackpool venue
articles.summary: A new promenade hotel and bar is being built on the site of the former Art Deco Yates building.
articles.body:
Work is finally under way to build a new promenade hotel and bar development on what was once a landmark Art Deco style building on the land in Blackpool.

The original multi-million pound plans to regenerate the former Yates Wine Lodge in South Shore were scrapped as long-term deterioration of its concrete and steel structure meant the building could not be made safe - and had to be demolished in November last year.

Blackpool Council planners approved fresh proposals to build a new version of the hotel and bar in February.

This week the site became a hive of activity, with workmen making the site ready for construction to begin with a member of the team saying the building was expected to be completed by next year.

The project entails the erection of a three-storey building at 407-411 Promenade, the Local Democracy Reporting Service said.

A revised planning statement on behalf of the application, from architect firm Abbott Hull Associates, stated: "The replacement building is to be of the same scale and footprint, together with a change of use to a hotel and drinking establishment with extended food provision.

"The proposal includes ancillary dining and events space, an additional storey, a roof terrace, a front canopy with roof terrace above, a three-storey rear extension, and a single-storey glazed rear seating area, along with external rendering and cladding."

Some 13 planning conditions were attached to the planning permission.

The former Yates bar on the Blackpool seafront was originally known as the Lion Hotel.

Opened in 1937 and designed by architect Halstead Best, it was a renowned Art Deco property with a circular tower and red brick façade before its closure and subsequent demolition.

In its heyday, the Yates was a busy venue and one of the most popular bars on South Shore seafront.

articles.title: In 2015, US engineers added blade deflectors to help turbines capture more wind; a wind-tunnel model’s power coefficient rose 10%, while a separate prototype test measured a 7.7% gain
articles.summary: Discover how Rutgers University engineers are enhancing wind turbine performance with innovative blade deflectors, achieving up to 10% increases in energy capture without needing larger turbines.
articles.body: The wind business has pursued size for most of the past few decades. Wider rotors, longer blades and taller towers have increased output, but they also bring heavier parts, more difficult transportation and costs that wind farm operators would rather avoid. A quieter question remains in the background as a result. Can turbines already spinning on farmland and hills capture a little more wind without getting bigger?Rutgers University engineers in New Jersey took up that question in a project whose final report was published in 2015. Arturo Villegas oversaw the project, which Rutgers CAIT, the university’s transportation and infrastructure research division, ran with funding through the US Department of Transportation’s University Transportation Centres program. His group created aerodynamic flow deflectors, small, slightly curved fins attached to turbine blades. According to the project summary, the team’s target was a 10% gain in power when the deflectors were added to new or existing turbines. Rutgers said a 1 MW turbine could rise from about $90,000 a year to $126,000, and early water-channel tests showed power increases of 8% to 12%.The power coefficient measures how much of the wind’s available power a turbine extracts. The theoretical ceiling, known as the Betz limit, is roughly 59%, and real machines fall well short of it. If a turbine converts a quarter of the energy in the wind, a 10% relative improvement will increase it to about 27.5%, which sounds small until you scale it up throughout a wind farm.How do deflectors work?Air doesn’t slide smoothly on a rotating blade. It also drifts sideways along it, from the root towards the tip. Conventional design views such drift as a loss. But the Rutgers team didn’t see it that way. They fastened fine silk threads to the blades of a miniature turbine, recorded them with a high-speed camera and saw that the airflow tilts by about 5 to 20 degrees. Their idea was to capture that sideways flow with a narrow, winglike deflector and convert it into more torque, the twisting force that drives the generator.Initially there were glimpses of hope. With trials in a tiny water channel showing roughly 8 to 12% power increases, the team turned to practical questions. The deflectors for the following tests were 3D printed and adhered with double-sided tape from 3M and Nitto, and in spin tests none of the tested tapes let loose. That out of the way, two proper trials ensued.Wind tunnel and field resultsThe first took place in the wind tunnel at Rutgers. Two identical 3D-printed turbines, each about 0.4 meters across, were tested at wind speeds from 3 to 6 meters per second, one with deflectors and one without. The second test was harder because it took place in real weather. The team transported a Whisper 100 turbine to the Wind Application Centre at Appalachian State University on Beech Mountain, North Carolina, at an altitude of around 1,556 meters, where typical winds at 30 meters are approximately 7 meters per second. It ran as is for two weeks. Then the team lowered the turbine tower and added the deflectors, and it ran for another two weeks. The final report, published by the US Department of Transportation, shows a 7.7% improvement in the average power coefficient over the entire curve. The best single point was at 8 metres per second, where the coefficient rose from 0.25 to 0.30, a 20% relative gain at that wind speed.One caveat is needed for a fair reading. The weather differed between the two fortnights: average wind speed at the main sensor was 4.48 meters per second before the deflectors and 5.38 after. The researchers normalized the measurements for air density and used an international testing standard for small turbines, but because the two runs were not simultaneous, the comparison is less controlled than a side-by-side test.What this could mean for wind farmsWhy would a few percent matter? The authors said a 2% increase in annual output can boost a wind farm’s profit by roughly 8%. They also noted that vortex generators, a retrofit currently on the market, often add 2% to 3%. The report included return-on-investment scenarios for a 1.5-megawatt turbine. Those figures were projections, not measurements, and should be read as such.The limitations matter too. So far, only two experiments have been carried out, one on a small model and one on a small turbine. The team itself proposes computer simulations and longer testing, first on turbines more than 10 meters across and then on full-scale machines over 100 meters, before anyone talks about commercial application. And it advises that a poorly formed or badly located deflector can actually decrease power rather than increase it.So the takeaway is a cautious one. Rutgers has shown that redirecting the sideways flow along a blade can contribute about 10% in a wind tunnel and 7.7% outdoors, enough to pique the interest of wind farm owners. The question is whether the same approach will work on a big turbine in real weather.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: In 2021, an investigation reported that Amazon’s Scottish warehouse sent millions of unsold or returned items, including TVs, laptops and books, to be destroyed each year
articles.summary: An investigation reveals Amazon's Scottish warehouse destroys millions of unsold or returned items each year, raising questions about waste in online retail.
articles.body: Every online order can create returns or unsold items that still need to be dealt with. As purchasing shifts to screens, returns have become commonplace, and someone has to decide what to do with a book that never sold or a laptop that was only opened once. The answer is not always what customers expect. That subject came into focus in June 2021 when ITV News filmed inside Amazon’s fulfilment centre in Dunfermline, Fife. ITV reported that the warehouse was destroying millions of unsold or returned items a year, including smart TVs, laptops and books. Amazon rejected that picture.In a statement to ITV, it said it was working toward a goal of zero product disposal, that its priority was to resell, donate or recycle unsold products, and that no items are sent to landfill in the UK. In the company’s account, returns are first inspected and, if they meet quality standards, relisted as new; if not, they can be routed to Amazon Warehouse, returned to suppliers or donated to charities. Amazon says most returned products can be resold this way, and that its UK donation partnership with In Kind Direct has reached more than 2,000 charities and volunteer organisations. The story reaches beyond one building in Scotland. It shows how the economics of online selling can push functional goods toward disposal. This article looks at what ITV reported, why it can happen and how governments are beginning to respond.What ITV reportedSecret footage from a former employee shows smart TVs, computers, drones, hairdryers, headphones, computer drives, novels and thousands of sealed face masks being sorted into crates marked for destruction. A leaked document showed that more than 124,000 items were tagged for destruction in one week in April, compared with just 28,000 marked for donation.The former worker said the usual target was to destroy about 130,000 items a week, and ITV said the total could reach 200,000 in some weeks. The same worker estimated that half of the items were still in their shrink wrap and that the rest were customer returns in good condition. ITV said it followed lorries carrying the goods to a landfill site and to recycling centres, and it published its findings on Amazon Prime Day.Why destruction sometimes costs lessITV said the reason was largely storage fees. The longer items sit unsold in a fulfilment centre, the more their owners pay to store them. At some point it can become cheaper to dispose of the stock than to store it, especially if the items were shipped in from overseas. Many items in Amazon’s warehouses belong to outside sellers rather than Amazon itself, so the decision often hinges on the seller’s numbers rather than any desire to waste goods.Amazon’s answer was unequivocal. John Boumphrey, its UK country manager, told ITV before the broadcast that the number of items destroyed was extremely small and that the company was working toward zero product disposal. The company also denied that the waste went to landfill, saying the site ITV tracked the lorries to is part of the Dunfermline Recycling Centre. The landfill denial does not answer the broader claim that functional goods were being destroyed, because items sent for recycling are also taken apart rather than resold. The dispute persisted in part because both claims could be true at the same time. ITV’s estimates rested on one leaked document and one former employee, and Amazon said they did not reflect its wider practice.Reaction and new rulesThe report drew a response from ministers and MPs. Business Secretary Kwasi Kwarteng told ITV News he was “very surprised” by the findings and wanted to get to the bottom of what was happening. The Guardian reported that three Labour MPs wrote to demand a meeting with Amazon’s UK country manager. Amazon says it works with the national charity In Kind Direct, which organises donations of leftover products, and that its FBA Donations programme has passed more than 20 million products from sellers to charities globally.Other countries had taken a harder road. According to the French government’s service-public.fr portal, France prohibited the disposal of unsold non-food products from January 1, 2022. Electrical and electronic items and books were among the first categories covered, and by the end of 2023 the rule covered all product types. Companies that break it can be fined up to 15,000 euros, the portal says.The Dunfermline case concerns one warehouse, and its figures were contested. But it illustrated how storage costs and returns may make destruction cheaper than giving, and it put the topic of what happens to unsold products in the public spotlight. Rules like France’s are one way to alter such incentives.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.body: The White House on Friday listed investments worth over $10.87 trillion in the US, including more than $330 billion from India, placing the country among the leading investors in the American economy.The investment figures were displayed in a video played on a loop on the White House’s YouTube channel. The list included two separate entries for India, one showing investments worth $310 billion and another listing $20.5 billion.“Lo-fi beats & billion-dollar investments to build America's Golden Age. Sit back, relax & enjoy the soothing sound of trillions pouring into America this Friday,” the White House said in a post on X.The video also featured a $15 billion steel plant announced by Essar Group's Mesabi Metallics in Iowa. The overall investment tally includes commitments from foreign countries as well as private industry in the US. The White House did not immediately respond to queries on the investment figures.In March, US President Donald Trump announced that Reliance Industries was investing $300 billion to establish an oil refinery in Brownsville, Texas. In May, Indian industry announced plans to invest up to $20.5 billion in the US on the sidelines of the SelectUSA Investment Summit.Trump has repeatedly highlighted investment commitments as evidence of his administration's economic achievements.During public rallies ahead of the November 3 midterm elections, he has claimed that his administration secured more than $20 trillion in investments and commitments for the US economy.The investment showcase comes as the US faces a widening budget deficit and mounting concerns over its public debt.The federal budget deficit rose to $1.99 trillion in fiscal year 2026, up 12 per cent from $1.78 trillion in the previous year, according to data released by the Treasury Department on Friday.The deficit, which occurs when government spending exceeds revenue, reached its highest level since 2021.The widening shortfall comes amid concerns over the country's $40.3 trillion debt burden and rising inflation, even as borrowing costs climb.Refunds linked to Trump's tariffs, which were overturned, have further added to the budget gap, the report said. articles.title: Notre Dame faces first real test as unbeaten BYU hosts the Fighting Irish in top-10 clash
articles.summary: College Sports rankings face scrutiny as CJ Carr's undefeated Notre Dame hosts Bear Bachmeier's BYU Cougars in a top-10 college football clash.
articles.body: Rankings in college sports can be a bit misleading. It really is hard to say who has the best team. One week you can be great; the next, you can suffer. Everyone is relying on people who will go do almost anything other than play professionally. Teams carry over 50 players, and only two or three from most teams will advance to the professional ranks. Maybe more at some of the best schools. Tonight, we have the #2 team in the country taking on the #8. Do either deserve their ranking? Notre Dame comes into the game with a 6-0 record for the season, but I’ll be the first to tell you that I don’t believe in this team. I know there is plenty of talent on their roster, but they aren’t exactly challenged with their schedule. CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE Beating up on teams that will combine to have a losing record isn’t exactly a major accomplishment. Are CJ Carr’s 1,378 passing yards and 16 touchdowns as impressive as, say, Julian Sayin’s 1,772 yards and 17 touchdowns? Sayin has at least faced Iowa and Texas this season. This season, the Fighting Irish have played Wisconsin, Rice, Michigan State, Purdue, North Carolina and Stanford. That combination of teams isn’t the worst in football by any means, but they also aren’t ranked teams. They do have three teams coming up on their schedule who are ranked – today against BYU, Nov. 7 against Miami and Nov. 21 against SMU. They haven’t really had a challenge this season, and only one game could be considered remotely close with an 11-point victory. WHO'S REALLY PLAYED THE BEST THUS FAR THROUGH THE FIRST HALF OF THE COLLEGE FOOTBALL SEASON? BYU is coming into this game as the top team in the Big 12 and has a perfect record. So far this season, the Cougars have taken down Utah Tech, Arizona, Colorado State, TCU, and Iowa State. I’d argue that they have had a tougher schedule than what Notre Dame has faced. This team is built around a balance of passing and rushing, instead of being solely focused on one of those games. Bear Bachmeier, the quarterback, is completing over 65% of his passes for 1,033 yards and eight touchdowns. He has also pulled the ball down and run with it 36 times, second most on the team, and scored four touchdowns. Take him out of the game, and the team has three guys with over 20 carries, averaging over five yards per carry and seven touchdowns. I do wonder if the team will have any success against Notre Dame if they don’t get the ground game going to open the passing attack. Perhaps they will need to get the passing game going to open the running. The books seem to expect this to be a bit of a defensive battle. The total opened at 54.5, but it has been bet down to 46.5 points. The spread also started at 11.5 in favor of the Fighting Irish. I personally like BYU at home to make this a game. I think their defense can combat some of Notre Dame’s running game. I also think Bachmeier will make this a dynamic game for him. Give me BYU +10.5. articles.title: 'Arbitrary, unreasonable’: Actor Imran Khan moves Bombay high court to challenge 'leave India' notice
articles.summary: MUMBAI: Actor Imran Khan Pal, around 44, filed a petition before the Bombay high court on Saturday to challenge a 'leave India' notice issued to him by
articles.body: MUMBAI: Actor Imran Khan Pal, around 44, filed a petition before the Bombay high court on Saturday to challenge a 'leave India' notice issued to him by the Foreigners Regional Registration Officer (FRRO), Mumbai to leave India by October 28.His petition described the notice as “arbitrary, unreasoned and wholly misconceived’’ and against principles of natural justice as it was issued sans any hearing to him and flouts his fundamental rights to equality under Article 14 and to life under article 21 of the Indian constitution.The notice gave him 2 weeks to leave. Khan said he has been in India since he was 2 years old.He e-filed his petition on Saturday, and on the same day FRRO sent him a fresh notice this time a show cause notice why he should not be acted against under the law governing foreigners and the OCIs.Of the October 14 original notice, which he challenged, his petition says it is a “punitive executive action’’ where he is made a “scapegoat’’ and the notice appears to be for “extraneous’’ reasons to “stifle perceived dissent.’’The plea which will be mentioned likely next Monday. Articles 14 and 21 are constitutional guarantees available to even foreigners in India, it underscored. He was given no reasons nor any reasonable opportunity to be heard and the notice was issued directly, Khan says in his petition.The FRRO, an officer under the Bureau of Immigration, had within four days of a protest in Mumbai against the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls, where the actor was present, invoked the Immigration and Foreigners Act (IFA) 2025 to issue him the departure notice on October 14.The notice is based on “purported contravention of uncited provisions of the IFA and the Rules and Orders’’ under it, the petition states. The Petition says Khan has no criminal antecedents.Seeking urgent intervention of the HC to stay the notice, the petition filed through MZM Legal and its advocates Zulfi Memon, Parvez Memon and Chirag Naik, says its potential enforcement would be a “mockery of the principles of natural justice and the Constitution of India’’ .The Oct 14 'leave India' notice is completely silent on any instances of the contravention in question; any underlying order or data forming the basis for issuance of the order or even any Security Report .The “LIN is not a Bona Fide exercise of statutory authority, but a manifestly arbitrary, high-handed and grossly disproportionate abuse of power, vitiated by complete non-application of mind. It seeks to single out the Petitioner as a convenient scapegoat and make an example of him in furtherance of extraneous personal agendas with which he has no connection, whether to appease public opinion or to stifle perceived dissent,’’ the petition says“Such punitive executive action cannot be permitted to place’’ his “constitutional guarantees in abeyance’’ or “extinguish rights that may be curtailed only… through a fair, just and reasonable procedure.”The notice doesn’t disclose statutory contravention or the semblance of any due process, Khan’s petition adds.Khan said he “no association, affiliation or connection whatsoever with any organization or institution involved in organizing or participating in the protest against the incumbent chief election commissioner in Mumbai’’.His petition says the notice is a disproportionate and dastic action, not factoring his rights as an OCI and not looking at complete facts and deserves to be quashed.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Mumbai | Silver Rate in Mumbai | Bank Holidays in Mumbai | Public Holidays in Mumbai | Mumbai AQI | Weather in Mumbai | Petrol Price in Mumbai | Diesel Price in Mumbai | CNG Price in Mumbai | LPG Price in MumbaiStay updated with the latest Mumbai news. articles.title: Nepal PM, president stress unity and social harmony in Dashain messages
articles.summary: Nepal Prime minister Balendra Shah and president Ramchandra Paudel on Saturday conveyed their greetings to the people on Bada Dashain, also known as
articles.body: Nepal Prime minister Balendra Shah and president Ramchandra Paudel on Saturday conveyed their greetings to the people on Bada Dashain, also known as Vijaya Dashami, the country's biggest festival, highlighting its importance in fostering family ties, social harmony and national unity.Their messages were issued on Phulpati, the seventh day of the 15-day Dashain festival. The occasion signals the start of the main festive period, when government offices close and celebrations gather momentum across Nepal.In his message, Prime Minister Shah said his government was committed to generating employment opportunities and promoting prosperity within the country so that Nepalis would not be compelled to travel abroad in search of work, according to the news agency PTI.Describing Bada Dashain as a festival that brings families together, Shah said it strengthens relationships, encourages unity and fosters closer bonds among people. He noted that the festival's religious, cultural and social significance had also helped connect Nepalis living across different parts of the world.“The sky itself feels different, the earth carries a unique fragrance, and the surroundings become naturally filled with joy and exuberance,” he said, describing the festive atmosphere.Shah observed that Nepalis had continued to celebrate Dashain and preserve their religious, cultural and social traditions despite numerous challenges over the years.PM remembers victims of devastating floodsReferring to the recent devastating flash floods in Bhotekoshi, Shah said this year's festivities had arrived while the country was still mourning the loss of lives and damage caused by the disaster. The floods left 1,455 people dead, 5,285 missing and more than 13,000 rescued, according to the figures cited in his message.The prime minister offered prayers for those who lost their lives, wished the injured a speedy recovery and expressed condolences to the affected families. He added that the government was working urgently to rehabilitate people displaced by the disaster.Shah also highlighted the traditional exchange of tika and jamara during Dashain. Tika, a mixture of vermilion powder, curd and rice, and jamara, consisting of barley shoots, are received from elders as symbols of respect for senior family members and affection for younger relatives.Nepalis traditionally receive tika and jamara from elders on Dashami, the festival's tenth day, which falls on October 21 this year.President Paudel stresses harmony and cultural identityIn a separate message, president Ramchandra Paudel extended his wishes for happiness, peace, prosperity, good health and continued progress to Nepalis living both within the country and abroad.Paudel said that while Nepal's diverse ethnic and religious communities follow their own customs and traditions, Bada Dashain plays a significant role in bringing families together and promoting social harmony, forgiveness, goodwill and fraternity.He added that the festival helps strengthen unity across Nepal's geographical, cultural and linguistic diversity while safeguarding the country's cultural identity.You use AI every day. articles.title: Protesters clash with police during nationwide demonstrations in France
articles.summary: Thousands rally in Paris and other cities for demonstrations set to unite students, teachers, unions and ‘yellow vests’.
articles.body:
Protesters have clashed with police in cities across France as major rallies take place across the country.

Scuffles broke out on Saturday in the capital, Paris, between groups of protesters and police, who used tear gas to push back people wearing hoods and masks.

The demonstrations are set to unite students, teachers, trade unions, and the resurging ‘ yellow vest’ movement – remnants of the grassroots cost-of-living protests that shook France in 2018.

Large numbers of riot police were deployed in the Place de la Republique, a square northeast of the city centre, and surrounding streets on Saturday. Dozens of people were reportedly already detained.

Reporting from Paris, Al Jazeera’s Natacha Butler said “a lot” of stun grenades and tear gas were being used by police.

She said that what began as a peaceful protests “never really got started”, as police quickly moved to isolate protesters, effectively trapping them between police lines. “That is where some of the trouble began,” Butler said.

In the southern city of Marseille, meanwhile, local media reported that protesters breached the town hall and looted shops in the city’s commercial district, while in Lyon, media reports said the local tourism office was set ablaze.

This is a “key moment” for France, said Al Jazeera’s Rosie Birchard, reporting from the western French city of Rennes.

“There are budget negotiations going on; the French government is trying to find ways to curb its ballooning national debt, and there consequential presidential elections happening next year,” she said.

France’s Interior Ministry had recorded 140 protest actions across the country by midday on Saturday, with 32,800 participants. The ministry said over 250 people had been arrested nationwide so far.

Saturday’s protests against the rising costs of goods like fuel and food come on the back of weeks of rallies from French high school students, who took to the streets to protest poor conditions in their schools.

Some children who attended those high school protests reported serious injuries at the hands of police, including the case of one 15-year-old girl who lost a hand.

Beyond the clashes at some demonstrations, Saturday has also seen widespread peaceful protests, with unions, teachers, healthcare workers and regular citizens taking to the streets.

French “yellow vest” protesters – who took to the streets in nationwide protests from 2018 to 2020 to protest rising fuels costs – have also signalled that they will join the protests.

The yellow vests have been “trying to make a comeback”, Birchard said, and this “seems to be the moment”.

Bruno Cautres, a researcher at the Paris-based Center for Political Research, told Al Jazeera that Saturday’s events are a “culmination of different mobilisations” including students, teachers, nurses, farmers, yellow vests.

He said the French population is frustrated by high taxes combined with a significant national debt and deficit that prevent the government satisfying their demands: “The French are asking themselves where are we going as a country? How are we going to get out of this budget crisis?”

President Emmanuel Macron appealed for calm on Friday, the eve of the protests.

“There is a constitutional right to protest and to express oneself,” he said in Brussels. “But this right comes with the need to respect. Respect for people, respect for property, and therefore a commitment not to insult or destroy.”

Kim English, Philip English and two of their children - nine-year-old Jayden and 12-year-old Callum - died after their home in Birch Avenue was set on fire on Tuesday.

articles.title: Black ink, burnt posters: Congress workers vandalise BJP office in Ajmer over Madan Rathore's Pakistan remark
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Congress workers vandalised the BJP office in Rajasthan's Ajmer on Saturday, pasting posters, smearing them with black ink and writing slogans
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Congress workers vandalised the BJP office in Rajasthan's Ajmer on Saturday, pasting posters, smearing them with black ink and writing slogans on the walls to protest against state BJP president Madan Rathore's controversial remarks about Pakistan. The protesters also burnt Rathore's posters and put up Youth Congress flags at the BJP office.The Youth Congress workers raised slogans against Rathore and attempted to throw black ink on the office signboard. The protest followed a row over his remarks that he would support Pakistan if it played against the US, as Pakistan was India's neighbour.Youth Congress coordinator Mohit Malhotra accused Rathore of supporting Pakistan. Defending the protest, he said it was against the BJP leader's remarks in support of the neighbouring country."If Madan Rathore supports Pakistan, he should go to Pakistan," news agency PTI reported quoting Mohit Malhotra.The Congress also shared a video of the protest on social media, accusing the BJP of showing support for Pakistan. "Rajasthan BJP President Madan Rathore has spoken of supporting that Pakistan which orchestrated the murder of Indian citizens," the party said in its post."Against this Pakistan love of the BJP, IYC comrades raised a massive ruckus outside the BJP office," it added."It is clear that treason and betrayal run through every vein of the BJP, the proof of which is once again before us," the post said. "Such anti-national thinking cannot be forgiven."The controversy began on Thursday when Rathore addressed a seminar at the BJP's state headquarters to mark the birth anniversary of former president APJ Abdul Kalam. He said he would support Pakistan if it played against the US because Pakistan was India's neighbour.Rathore also said that people who burst crackers to celebrate India's defeat against Pakistan could not be considered patriots.Following the backlash, Rathore said his remarks had been distorted and presented out of context.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Imagine Sisyphus posting: The absurd economics of India’s creator boom
articles.summary: When Albert Camus wrote that one must imagine Sisyphus happy, he was not, one would assume, thinking of India's content creator economy.
articles.body: When Albert Camus wrote that one must imagine Sisyphus happy, he was not, one would assume, thinking of India's content creator economy. And yet, there is something Sisyphean about the business of being a creator: the endless filming, editing, posting and chasing of engagement, only to start all over again the next day.One must imagine the creator successful. But is success really within reach of everyone who has been promised a shot at it? In a world where almost everyone has some form of digital access to social media, is the creator economy truly sustainable or even democratised?For a country as young, populous and linguistically diverse as India, the proposition of a platform like social media has always been transformative, for the common man and the common company. Talent could emerge from anywhere, audiences could be found beyond geographical boundaries, and businesses could reach consumers through hyperlocal advertising at a fraction of the cost of traditional campaigns.According to a 2025 report by Boston Consulting Group (BCG), India has between 2 million and 2.5 million active digital creators, whose content influences an estimated $350–400 billion (Rs 33.24 lakh crore to Rs 38 lakh crore) in annual consumer spending. That figure is projected to exceed $1 trillion (Rs 94.97 lakh crore) by 2030.A 2024 YouTube Culture and Trends survey, conducted with research firm SmithGeiger, also found that 83% of surveyed Indians aged 14–24 identified themselves as creators. But identifying as a creator is not the same as earning a living from it.And within this framework the most pertinent question comes up, has just the ability to become a creator been democratised far more than the ability to make a living as one. And who is it that gets to make a living out of it?A booming economy, a crowded marketplaceThe numbers suggest an industry expanding on almost every front. But the growth of the creator economy has also brought more people into competition for brand partnerships, audience attention and a share of the same advertising budgets. The money flowing in the market is not able to keep pace with the number of people wanting to profit off of it.Speaking on the basis of anonymity to a marketing manager from a small digital marketing agency based out of Gurgaon, TOI learnt that in a lot of cases almost 70% upwards of a brand’s marketing budget is allocated for influencer marketing.Micro- and nano-influencers are particularly attractive to brands and agencies because they can offer targeted audience engagement at lower rates than larger creators. But the economics of these collaborations do not always work in creators’ favour. Agencies, acting as middlemen, can negotiate deals that leave creators with little or no monetary compensation. In many cases, instead of being paid for their work, creators are offered barter collaborations, receiving products or services in exchange for promotional content. Others face such long delays in receiving their remuneration that they eventually give up on being paid altogether. The result is a growing market in which brands can benefit from creators’ reach and labour without necessarily paying for either.The gap between influence and monetisation is apparent in BCG’s estimates. In FY24, creators influenced $350–400 billion (Rs 33.24 lakh crore to Rs 38 lakh crore) in consumer spending in India, while the creator economy generated $20–25 billion (Rs 1.90 lakh crore to Rs 2.38 lakh crore) for participants, including platforms and creators. The figures are not directly comparable measures of money flowing between parties, but they underline the distinction between the spending creators' influence and the revenue generated within the ecosystem.The broader data suggests that this gap exists alongside a rapidly expanding market. A 2024 report by EY projected that India’s influencer marketing industry would reach Rs 3,375 crore by 2026, up from an estimated Rs 1,275 crore in 2022. The industry, then, is attracting greater marketing investment, but that does not automatically translate into more paid opportunities for individual creators.A 2026 study by the Indian School of Business, in collaboration with creator marketing platform Hashfame, found that India's creator base grew from 9.6 lakh in 2020 to 41.2 lakh in 2025.But the supply of creators appears to be growing faster than campaign opportunities. Among non-metro creators, the campaign-to-creator ratio fell from approximately 0.37 in 2020 to 0.10 in 2025. Brand collaborations are not expanding in proportion to the growing creator base.BCG data suggests that out of the entire influencer pool in India, 8-10 per cent of creators are able to monetise their content effectively, and an average income they generate is close to only Rs 18,000 a month.The business modelA creator’s job is to be seen by the people for the work they produce. In the current digital climate there are upwards of 200 million creators and the number is constantly growing. This is why visibility is such a core tenet in this economy, but visibility does not guarantee a salary.Platforms like Instagram do not have a universal, fixed payment for every view available to every Indian creator. So one may suggest that the platform is democratised, everyone can generate views, but not everyone can monetise those views. A small elitist per cent of creators usually dominate when it comes to earnings.Building an audience and viewership is also a daily job. Talking to 13 different people who tried their hand at becoming a creator and then ended up discarding that effort, TOI found out that a lot of them spent money in the hopes of future returns. But when the returns never came, they had to discard their efforts before it became even more expensive for them to sustain it. One of the people questioned even spent Rs 1.8 lakhs on getting a new phone because she felt like it could boost how her content looked. Till date she has not made any money through her social media.Her experience points to a less visible cost of the creator economy: the money, time and labour people invest before they have any assurance that their work will pay off. For those who never manage to monetise their audience, the pursuit of visibility can become an expense rather than a livelihood.The uncertainty does not necessarily disappear once a creator builds an audience. Macro-influencer Ved Maddison, who has 324,000 followers, argues that even at this level, content creation may not generate a sustainable income, particularly in an expensive city such as Mumbai. Maddison has carved out a niche as a mixed creator who is white-passing while retaining other cultural markers of his Indian identity. But his experience also draws attention to a less visible advantage: he had a financial safety net when he began his career.That cushion matters in an industry where building an audience can take time, returns are uncertain and creators may have to keep investing before they earn anything back. A platform may allow anyone to publish content, but not everyone can afford to keep doing so until it becomes profitable.Having a niche is itself becoming more complicated as the creator economy expands. With more people entering the market and people increasingly identifying with the creator label, the competition is no longer just for audience attention, but for the distinctiveness that makes a creator worth following in the first place. How long can a niche remain a niche before someone else finds a way to replicate it, repackage it or do it better? This leaves creators under constant pressure to put themselves out there, keep their audiences engaged and remain attractive to brands.This has implications for the content itself. When posting becomes a daily requirement, creators have less room to experiment, develop ideas or let a piece of work take shape at its own pace. Over time, the demand for constant output can risk diminishing the very creativity that made a creator worth following in the first place.Scrutinising the language of democratisationIt would be misleading to conclude that the creator economy is simply a market in which everyone loses. Its growth has created new ways for people to find audiences, build businesses and reach consumers.The problem is that these outcomes are not distributed evenly. A platform can make publishing accessible to millions without providing them with a dependable source of income.This is also why the language of democratisation needs closer scrutiny. Social media has lowered some of the barriers that once separated creators from audiences. But access to a platform is not the same as access to the resources, networks and commercial opportunities that make the platform profitable. Nor does the ability to publish content mean that everyone has an equal chance of turning it into a livelihood.The distinction is between democratising participation and democratising returns. The former is visible in the growing number of creators and the expansion of content beyond India's largest cities. The latter is harder to establish, particularly when only a small proportion of active creators monetise effectively and many depend on irregular brand deals.That does not make the creator economy a failed experiment. It makes the promise of the creator economy more complicated than its most optimistic projections suggest. Its success cannot be measured only by the amount of consumer spending influenced by creators, the number of people posting videos or the money brands allocate to campaigns. It must also be measured by whether creators can earn enough, consistently enough, to sustain the work they do.When Camus asked us to imagine Sisyphus happy, he was writing about the absurdity of a task that must be repeated without end. The creator, too, returns to the same cycle: filming, editing, posting, learning what resonates and beginning again. Sisyphus pushed his rock for eternity. Unlike him, the creator's burden is not simply the endless work, but the belief that somewhere along the climb lies a payoff that remains elusive for most.You use AI every day. articles.body: NEW DELHI: A criminal complaint has been filed against Lok Sabha leader of opposition Rahul Gandhi by woman journalist Richa Parasar, who has sought FIR against the Congress leader.Parasar has alleged mistreatment, threats and use of criminal force against her while she was reporting on a protest near the Supreme Court on October 12, 2026.Parashar, who said she was three months pregnant, has alleged that Rahul Gandhi 'grabbed her hand' and 'pulled her' forward before his security personnel pushed her away while she was covering the INDIA bloc's protest against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar on October 12.Parashar claimed she fell down the steps, landed on her stomach, injured her hand and knees, and broke her phone."I extended the mic and they made a gesture so I move it but I saw other mic IDs being pushed so I also put mine…Rahul Gandhi moved forward with a nasty expression, he grabbed my hand and pulled me forward and then his bodyguards pushed me…I fell down the stairs of Supreme Court, falling on my face," Parashar said in a video recorded from her hospital bed, with BJP leaders around her.Earlier, Parashar had shared a video on Instagram claiming she was 'pushed by the man who says Smash the Patriarchy'.She also alleged that the Congress MP pushed her cameraperson, who then fell on top of her, followed by several others amid the commotion due to the massive crowd."I did not ask him any questions nor did I say anything to him. I fell down the stairs and my cameraman fell on me and top of him 4 people also fell.I fell on my stomach. I got hurt on my hand and my phone broke, my knees also got hurt," she claimed.Parashar further alleged that Rahul's supporters shouted at her instead of helping her get up.She questioned the Congress's stand on women's safety and urged media organisations that had recorded the incident to release their footage.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Man killed, four injured in suspected militant attack on Kuki village in Manipur
articles.summary: A 36-year old man was killed and four others injured after suspected militants attacked Chassad village in Manipur's Kamjong district on Saturday,
articles.body: A 36-year old man was killed and four others injured after suspected militants attacked Chassad village in Manipur's Kamjong district on Saturday, triggering an exchange of fire between the assailants and a local armed group, police said.Several rounds were fired at the Kuki village around 2.30 pm, and the gunfight was continuing in the evening, a senior police officer said, according to PTI."Village head Thangjahou Haokip (48), and four others - Khailun Haokip, Seikhohou, Hegin Haokip and Seipao Haokip - were injured after the suspected militants attacked the village. All the injured were taken to a hospital where Seikhohou succumbed to his injuries," the officer said."The gunfight is still underway in the evening," the officer added.The Committee on Tribal Unity condemned the attack and urged the state government to deploy central forces in the area.The latest violence comes amid broader reported cases of violence. The escalating clashes between Kuki-Zo and Naga communities, which have claimed more than 50 lives since February, with homes and shops torched and civilians caught in attacks across several districts.Last week, nine people, including six Nagas, two Kukis and a Gorkha farmer, were killed in a series of attacks across three districts in a 12-hour period. The violence included an attack on Chassad village and gunfights in Kangpokpi and Ukhrul districts. Houses and shops were also set on fire, prompting prohibitory orders in Kamjong and a shutdown call on National Highway 202.The situation remained tense on Thursday, when a Kuki-Zo woman, Hatneikim Haokip, was killed and her husband injured in an alleged ambush by suspected Naga militants on the road between Phaikoh and Aishu in Kamjong district. Two other people travelling with them were reported missing. The woman was reportedly travelling with the group to buy essential commodities.The violence has also affected Kamjong, Ukhrul, Kangpokpi, Tamenglong, Noney and other districts, raising concerns over security in the state and along the India-Myanmar border.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.body: Agartala: To boost onion availability and stabilise prices during the festive season, the Department of Consumer Affairs has extended its rail distribution network to Tripura, launching the Kanda Express service to Agartala with around 440 metric tonnes of buffer onions, said state civil supplies minister Sushanta Chowdhury on Saturday.The consignment, funded through the Centre’s Price Stabilisation Fund, is expected to reach Agartala on Sunday. The move aims to strengthen supply chains, raise market stocks and ensure onions are sold at reasonable rates during peak demand.After routing buffer onions to Assam via the dedicated rail service, the Centre has now added Tripura as another rail-linked destination, creating an additional channel for essential food supplies. Seven districts—Dhalai, South Tripura, Khowai, Unakoti, West Tripura, Gomati and Sepahijala—are expected to benefit through a rail-and-road distribution plan.More than 2,800 MT was sent to the northeast through two rakes and 44 trucks, officials said. articles.title: Trump aide Susie Wiles helped set up ‘sanctioned hit’ on fired White House press secy Katie Zacharia: Report
articles.summary: White House chief of staff Susie Wiles helped arrange a tough Fox News interview with former White House press secretary Katie Zacharia, which was
articles.body: White House chief of staff Susie Wiles helped arrange a tough Fox News interview with former White House press secretary Katie Zacharia, which was described by sources as a “sanctioned hit”, hours before she was removed from the role, according to reports.Zacharia appeared on Sean Hannity’s primetime show on Thursday, where she faced questions about her legal credentials and her brief, troubled stint as White House press secretary. She struggled to defend her record, including her claim to be a lawyer despite failing the California bar exam in 2011.According to The Telegraph, citing people familiar with the matter, Wiles helped set up the interview because Zacharia was not her preferred choice to replace Karoline Leavitt. One source described the appearance as a “sanctioned hit” on the former press secretary.A person familiar with the internal dynamics told Politico that Wiles and Hannity were friendly and spoke often.However, a senior White House official rejected the suggestion that Wiles had deliberately set Zacharia up for a difficult interview. “Susie and Sean do talk, but Susie did not need to feed her to Sean or anybody else. It’s not her style,” the official said, according to The Telegraph and Politico.The official added that Hannity’s interview was not the decisive factor in Zacharia’s exit, pointing instead to her earlier appearance on Fox & Friends and her answers about her legal qualifications.White House communications director Steven Cheung also dismissed reports of Wiles’ involvement as speculation, saying the claims were “fiction that’s not even creative”. He added that Zacharia would continue supporting President Donald Trump as she transitioned to a new role.What happened during the Fox News interview?During the interview, Hannity directly asked Zacharia whether she had taken but failed the bar exam. She replied, “Correct, yes Sean.”Zacharia explained that she graduated from Pepperdine University School of Law and sat for the California bar exam in 2011, but did not pass. She said she had been preparing to move to China with her husband and considered the result “inconsequential”.She also said she later worked in the international practice division of a Chinese law firm, handling cross-border corporate transactions, where admission to a US state bar was not required.Asked about social media posts identifying her as an attorney, Zacharia said she believed they were reposts and that she had corrected the record. She maintained that she had consulted legal professionals who advised her she could describe herself as a “lawyer”, though not an “attorney”.The controversy had intensified after her first White House press briefing, which Hannity described as widely criticised. The briefing lasted about 14 minutes and included three questions.Fox News Media said Hannity independently decides whom to interview and what questions to ask.A Fox News source told The Telegraph that Zacharia’s own performance, rather than an orchestrated effort to push her out, had undermined her position.Trump said he asked Zacharia to reconsiderTrump confirmed on Friday that he had advised Zacharia to reconsider whether she wanted to continue as press secretary, saying she had been treated unfairly by the media.“She was on Sean Hannity last night. articles.title: Girl, 6, alerts neighbours after 3-yr-old brother beaten; mom, stepdad arrested
articles.summary: Raipur: Mom, stepdad arrested after 3-year-old allegedly beaten and burned; 6-year-old sister alerted neighbours. Child recovering under protection care.
articles.body: RAIPUR: A three-year-old boy allegedly beaten repeatedly by his stepfather and burned with cigarettes is recovering under child-protection care after police arrested his mother and stepfather following a complaint by residents of Tarun Nagar, Lodhipara. The case came to light after the boy’s six-year-old sister alerted neighbours to the alleged abuse.The alleged assault took place around 8.30am on Oct 13, when the boy and his sibling were allegedly subjected to violence by their stepfather. The matter came to light when the girl reportedly told residents that her younger brother had been beaten. Concerned about the boy’s condition, residents approached Civil Lines police and submitted a collective complaint on Oct 15, following which an FIR was registered late that night.The complaint alleged that the stepfather had repeatedly assaulted the boy and that his mother failed to intervene. Residents reported that the child had swelling around his left eye, injuries on his face and body, and a plaster cast on one hand. Police said the boy had sustained serious injuries to his face, around his eye and other parts of his body, besides cigarette burns.Residents further alleged that the couple’s other two children were also subjected to mistreatment and were sometimes denied food. They expressed concern that the children could remain vulnerable if they continued living in the same circumstances, particularly if the family left its rented accommodation following police action.The residents sought immediate intervention by the police and child-protection authorities, including a medical examination of the injured boy and an assessment of the children’s safety. They also urged that the children be presented before the Child Welfare Committee (CWC), Raipur, for appropriate care and protection.The station house officer told TOI that intoxication was a factor in the alleged assault. The three-year-old is now under child-protection care, and his condition is improving, police said.Police alleged that the mother supported the stepfather instead of intervening to stop the violence and attempted to conceal the incident. After questioning the complainant and witnesses, police arrested the stepfather, 35, and the mother, 40. Both allegedly admitted to their involvement during questioning, police said.Civil Lines police registered a case (Crime No. 543/2026) under Sections 115(2) and 3(5) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita and Section 75 of the Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2015. articles.summary: Varkala police found 17 of 20 spas operating without licences during pre-season inspections; shutdown action initiated and municipality notified.
articles.body: T’puram: Varkala Police on Saturday found 17 spas functioning without mandatory licences and authorisation documents during inspections held ahead of the tourist season.The drive was conducted on the directions of Rural SP Prasanthan Kani B K to check whether spa centres in the tourist destination had secured the required permissions. Officers inspected 20 establishments across the Varkala areas.Varkala DSP P V Ramesh Kumar said 17 centres failed to produce valid documents needed to operate. articles.title: In 2022, Wyoming landowner Paul Hughes rejected a $3,600-an-acre easement offer; four years later, the board behind an $80 million reservoir is considering eminent domain to secure the last land it needs
articles.summary: In 2022, Wyoming landowner Paul Hughes rejected a proposal offering $3,600 per acre for an easement connected to the proposed Alkali Creek Reservoir near
articles.body: In 2022, Wyoming landowner Paul Hughes rejected a proposal offering $3,600 per acre for an easement connected to the proposed Alkali Creek Reservoir near Hyattville. Four years later, the Nowood Watershed Improvement District, which is developing the roughly $80 million project, is considering eminent domain to secure the remaining land rights it needs. According to the Basin Republican-Rustler, Hughes said the 2022 offer was the only one he had ever received.The dispute has turned a local water project into a broader test of property rights, public infrastructure, and the limits of eminent domain. The reservoir is intended to store water for late-season irrigation, but landowners who have not signed easement agreements say the project would benefit downstream users while placing burdens on those whose land lies above the reservoir site.What the reservoir would doThe proposed Alkali Creek Dam and Reservoir would impound 8,000 acre-feet of water from Medicine Lodge and Paint Rock creeks. Its primary purpose is to provide late-season irrigation for 35 irrigating families in the region.The project has been under discussion for about 15 years. It has also become increasingly expensive, with cost estimates rising from an initial $20 million to as much as $113 million, while legislators have appropriated $59 million so far, as per the report.The Wyoming Water Development Office and Commission have spent about $8 million on the project, but construction has not begun. The main obstacle is the lack of completed easements from a small number of neighbouring landowners.The easements still neededOnly 13 acres of permanent easements and 34 acres of temporary easements remain outstanding, according to state Senator Dan Laursen. Those relatively small areas have nonetheless stalled a project that has been planned for years. Easements do not necessarily transfer ownership of the land. They can give a project developer the right to build, operate, maintain, or access infrastructure across a property, often in exchange for payment or other negotiated terms.For the Alkali Creek project, the easements would include a permanent right of way to operate the Anita Ditch as a pipeline feeding the reservoir. They would also include temporary construction easements needed during building work.Hughes rejected the 2022 offerPaul Hughes rejected the $3,600-per-acre easement proposal in 2022. According to the Basin Republican-Rustler, he said it was the only proposal he had received for the project. His rejection matters because the reservoir project cannot move forward without the necessary land rights. The fact that a small number of landowners have declined to sign has left the Nowood Watershed Improvement District with a limited number of options.The dispute has also raised questions about whether the initial offer reflected the value landowners place on their property, access, privacy, and future control. For rural landowners, an easement can affect more than a single acre because construction, maintenance, and access may alter how land is used over time.Eminent domain enters the discussionThe Nowood Watershed Improvement District has told at least two ranch owners that it expects to begin eminent domain proceedings if they decline a final easement offer. The letters gave recipients 15 days to respond and proposed easements across seven acres for a total of $19,255, subject to an updated appraisal.Eminent domain, also called condemnation, allows a government or authorised public entity to acquire private property rights for public use, generally with compensation. It remains one of the most controversial tools in infrastructure development because it can override a landowner’s refusal to sell.Wyoming Water Development Office Director Jason Mead described condemnation as the “nuclear option”, as per the report. That language reflects how politically sensitive the issue has become, even among supporters of the reservoir.A project with growing costsThe Alkali Creek project has drawn criticism because its cost has increased sharply over time. Legislators have appropriated $59 million, while estimates have ranged from $20 million to as much as $113 million.The Wyoming Water Development Commission has spent roughly $8 million on the project without construction beginning. The Nowood Watershed Improvement District has also spent $1.6 million in state funds on property and easements at the Mercer ranch, where the dam and reservoir would be located.The state legislature set a July 1, 2027, deadline for securing the easements. Lawmakers who opposed the project wanted a stricter deadline and attempted to prohibit the use of eminent domain for the project, but those efforts failed, as per reports.Why landowners are pushing backSome landowners say the reservoir’s location creates an unfair distribution of benefits and burdens. Those who have not signed easement agreements are located above the reservoir site and would not be able to use the water it stores.Landowner representative Shirran summarised the concern by saying, as per the report, “You can’t put water back upstream.” The comment captures the central objection: landowners above the dam may lose land rights or face construction impacts without receiving the irrigation benefits that downstream users would gain.The dispute is therefore not simply about money. It is also about whether a project designed to serve a specific group of irrigators should be allowed to use eminent domain against neighbours who do not directly benefit from it.What happens nextThe Nowood Watershed Improvement District has said, it was reported, that it will reluctantly initiate eminent domain proceedings if landowners decline its final offers. That means the dispute could move from negotiation into a legal process that determines whether the easements are necessary for a public purpose and how much compensation is owed.The outcome will matter well beyond Hughes and the other holdout landowners. It could shape how future water projects in Wyoming approach easement negotiations, compensation, and the use of condemnation.For now, the Alkali Creek Reservoir remains stalled at the same point it has faced for years. The project has funding, approvals, and a deadline, but it still needs the cooperation of a small number of landowners whose property sits in its path.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient.
